It will depend. If you have complete access to secure boot and all EFI configurations so you can clear their keys and generate your own, go for it. If secure boot is locked down so you can't change keys, even if its in an unlocked state to allow OS installation, fucking run.

As for the windows shitware and spyware they got caught installing, The difference between them and other OEMs is the getting caught part. As long as you have complete access to the EFI and secure boot settings it won't matter once you install linux.

On the subject of IME, aka "intel has rewtkits on all cpus!". Once again, with linux you would need to install a bunch of extra stuff related to IPMI, including kernal modules, to be accessible/exploitable from inside the OS in a meaningful way, and it aint something that comes in the standard Linux install (MAYBE enterprise level distros.)

When you buy it, get a cheap ass ~4gb thumb drive too, first thing to do is trash any predefined secure boot settings (this kills the default OEM Windows install.) and generate your own keys to store on your cheap new thumb drive and store it in a safe place. This should be the first thing you do when you plug the computer in before anything else. That will make sure YOU are the authority for your bootloader and bios access, not Lenovo or MS.

The Empire of Mali, In Our Time - BBC Radio 4

Melvyn Bragg and guests discuss the Empire of Mali which flourished from 1200 to 1600 and was famous in the wider world for the wealth of rulers such as Mansa Musa. Mali was the largest empire in west Africa and for almost 400 years controlled the flow of gold from mines in the south up to the Mediterranean coast and across to the Middle East. These gold mines were the richest known deposits in the 14th Century and produced around half of the world's gold. When Mansa Musa journeyed to Cairo in 1324 as part of his Hajj, he distributed so much gold that its value depreciated by over 10%. Some of the mosques he built on his return survive, albeit rebuilt, such as the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Great Mosque of Djenne.
